You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

The failing test is `testLargeSample()` in `PolynomialFitterTest`. It attempts to fit polynomials of degree 0 to 9 using 40000 observed points with noise. The test checks that the relative error in the fitted polynomial is less than 0.01 for many points in [-1, 1].

The bug report states that new multivariate vector optimizers cannot handle a large number of weights because an nxn full matrix is created and copied when passing n weights, causing memory exhaustion for large n (e.g., 4120 data points). This issue manifests when fitting curves like polynomial curve fitters with large data points.

Looking at the code snippet of `PolynomialFitter.fit(double[])` (line 109-111), it delegates the fitting call to `fit(ParametricUnivariateFunction, double[])` method from `PolynomialFitter`, specifically passing a `PolynomialFunction.Parametric` as the function and the initial guess array.

The `fit` method invoked eventually calls some optimizer (likely the Levenberg-Marquardt optimizer), which internally requires Jacobian computation and uses weights matrices, potentially causing large memory consumption when many data points (weights) exist.

In this case, the test calls `fitter.addObservedPoint(1.0, x, y)` for 40000 points, which likely stores all these points and weights internally, then runs `fitter.fit(init)`. Because of the large number (40000) of observed points, internally when the optimizer constructs the weight or covariance matrix, a dense nxn matrix of size 40000x40000 might be created, exhausting available memory, as described in the bug report.

Hence the root cause is the internal design of the `PolynomialFitter` combined with the optimizer used: passing a large number of observed points causes the Levenberg-Marquardt optimizer (or underlying vector optimizers) to allocate large full matrices proportional to the number of points, which is inefficient and unscalable.

The test fails because this leads to either memory exhaustion or performance degradation, or it triggers an internal error due to large matrix operations with weights.

Recent bug reports on optimizer parameter changes or new optimizer API are unrelated.

# Diagnosis

The failure is caused by the internal behavior of the vector optimizers, used by `PolynomialFitter`, which create and copy a full nxn weight matrix when fitting models with large numbers of data points. In the test, 40000 observed points trigger this memory-intensive operation, causing failures. This is consistent with the bug report that highlights the memory exhaustion caused by the new optimizer handling of weights in curve fitting scenarios with large data. The problem stems from the fact that passing a large number of weights to multivariate vector optimizers results in full matrices being created, which is not scalable or efficient.

The `PolynomialFitter.fit()` method uses the optimizer internally, and the optimizer or the weight-handling logic is responsible for this large matrix handling.

To fix, changes are needed in the weight management in the optimizer or fitter to prevent constructing full large matrices when only diagonal or sparse weights are needed. Possibly the weight representation or the optimizer internals should be optimized to handle large weight vectors without full matrix expansions.

---

Next, I will identify the optimizer class and the weight handling classes used by the polynomial fitter during fitting to pinpoint exact methods responsible for this behavior.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
